director.chapterArc: A clinical confrontation where the protagonist, exhausted and stripped of his tools, learns that saving his brother requires a lifetime of dependency rather than a quick fix.
director.restraintNote: The narrator must maintain absolute neutrality. The horror is in the facts: dead bone, permanent limp, thirteen years of obligation. Do not dramatize; let the arithmetic speak for itself.

cues.delivery: Measured urgency. Sowerby is efficient but not cold; he delivers the diagnosis with a rhythm that mimics his own professional speed.
cues.from: Doctor Sowerby came out at the eighth hour with a folder under his arm and found him on the bench.
cues.through: "The trouble is what got in through the skin when it happened. There's an infection in the bone. Not round it. In it. It's been in there the better part of two months and it has killed a piece of that bone, and the piece is dead, and dead bone doesn't come back and medicine doesn't reach into it, because there's nothing alive in there for the blood to carry medicine along. It sits in the leg being a place for the infection to live, and it will go on doing that for as long as it's in him, and while it's in him he will keep having the nights you have been sitting up through, until one of them doesn't stop."
cues.reason: Shift from narrator observation to character voice for Doctor Sowerby's exposition.

cues.delivery: Flat delivery of the 'bill'. The doctor is stating a permanent reality. No pity in the voice; only factual weight.
cues.from: "Now the bill," said Doctor Sowerby, "and I'm going to do the money part in four words, because it's four words. It doesn't cost anything.
cues.through: "And he'll be coming back through those doors every year until he's done growing, for somebody to measure him."
cues.reason: Shift to Doctor Sowerby's explanation of the long-term consequences.

cues.delivery: Internal monologue. The narrator must slow slightly to let the arithmetic of 'thirteen years' land without melodrama.
cues.from: Jab sat on the bench and did the arithmetic, because his head would not do anything else, and had never once in seventeen years done anything else, and had got him and his brother four hundred miles.
cues.reason: Shift to Jab's internal realization and acceptance.

cues.delivery: Senna's voice. Tired but sharp. She is a mirror to Jab; her tone should be observational and grounded.
cues.from: "You're the brother," said a voice from across the ward.
cues.through: "Yes," said Senna. "I heard that too. This room has no walls in it worth the name and I have got very good at pretending to be asleep."
cues.reason: Shift to character dialogue for Senna.

cues.delivery: Tonk's voice. Small and immediate. Jab's response must be gentle but firm.
cues.from: "It was ages," said Tonk, and Jab sat up and looked at his brother, who was grey and small and flat in a white bed with a tube in the back of his hand and his eyes half open, and who was, for the first time in eleven days, not making the sound he made on the out-breath.
cues.reason: Shift to character dialogue for the final exchange.

pauses.reason: Emphasis on the least of it.

pauses.after: "I thought you might," said Doctor Sowerby. "About four in five, for the infection, first time of asking. Of the one in five, most get there at the second operation. A few don't get there at all, and for those it's the leg, and I'm saying that out loud in this corridor rather than letting you find it under a door at three in the morning."
pauses.reason: Speaker reset after the doctor's statistic about survival rates.
Emphasis on the first part of the bill (money).

pauses.before: He is going to pay for this leg for the rest of his life.
The place a child's leg grows from

pauses.after: "And he'll be coming back through those doors every year until he's done growing, for somebody to measure him."
pauses.reason: Major emotional landing: The finality of 'every year until he's done growing'.

pauses.after: He had carried his brother out of the home valley to save his life, and he had, and the price was that neither of them was ever going home.
pauses.reason: Speaker reset after Jab accepts the price (never going home).

pauses.after: He was asleep. Somebody had washed him — all of him, his hair too, which was lying flat and dark and clean on a pillow instead of standing up in the two directions it had stood up in for six weeks. There was a needle in the back of his hand with a tube going up to a bag on a hook. The leg was out from under the blanket in a padded trough with the wrapping off, and Jab, who had not seen it in a proper light in seven weeks, looked at it for four seconds and then looked at the window.
pauses.reason: Scene turn: The visual of Tonk's leg exposed and clean.

pauses.after: "It was ages," said Tonk, and Jab sat up and looked at his brother, who was grey and small and flat in a white bed with a tube in the back of his hand and his eyes half open, and who was, for the first time in eleven days, not making the sound he made on the out-breath.
pauses.reason: Speaker reset after Jab acknowledges the time passed ('ages').
Emphasis on Tonk's perception of time.
